items.prose: An undirected graph has 10 nodes, 15 edges and no self-loops.
items.question: How many entries do its adjacency lists hold in total?

feedback.correct: Each edge is listed at both ends: 30.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many lists one edge appears in.

byKey.once: You counted each edge once. An undirected edge appears in both its ends' lists.
byKey.plus: That is $V + E$, the big O size. The entries alone are $2E$.
byKey.sq: That is the matrix's cell count, $V^2$.

explain.text: Edge u–v puts v in u's list and u in v's. So the lists hold $2E = 30$ entries, plus one key per node.

items.prose: BFS from P, taking neighbours in alphabetical order.
items.question: Put the nodes in the order BFS processes them.

feedback.correct: P, Q, S, R, T, U.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Finish every node at distance 1 before any at distance 2.

byKey.R: R is two edges from P. Q and S, both one edge away, come first.

explain.text: P's neighbours Q and S come first. Then their new neighbours R and T, in the order Q and S were found. U is three edges away, so it is last.

items.prose: Recursive DFS from P on the same graph, neighbours in alphabetical order.
items.question: In what order does it first reach the nodes?

options.text: P, Q, R, U, T, S
P, Q, S, R, T, U
options.why: That is the BFS order. DFS keeps going from Q before it ever looks at S.

options.text: P, S, T, U, R, Q
options.why: That is a stack version pushing neighbours in sorted order, so the largest comes off first. Recursion takes Q first.

feedback.correct: It goes round the long way: Q, R, U, T, and S last.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep going from the newest node.

explain.text: From P the first neighbour is Q, then R, then U. From U, T is new, and from T, S. Every node is reached before the search backs up.

items.prose: Land is 1, water is 0. Cells join only through a shared side.
items.question: How many islands are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Join cells only through shared sides.

byKey.diag: You joined cells meeting at a corner. r3c1 touches r2c2 only diagonally.
byKey.cells: You counted land cells, not groups.

explain.text: Top left: r1c1, r1c2, r2c2; top right: r1c5, r2c4, r2c5. Bottom left: r3c1, r4c1, r4c2, and r4c4 alone. Corner contacts do not join.

items.prose: Arrows: load → clean, clean → features, load → calendar, calendar → features, features → model.
items.question: Which order is **not** valid?

options.why: This one is valid: each arrow points forward. features comes after both clean and calendar.
This one is valid: features waits for clean and calendar, and both come earlier.

feedback.correct: features runs before calendar, one of its inputs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each arrow against each order.

explain.text: features needs both clean and calendar. The first order runs it before calendar, so it uses a missing input. The other two respect every arrow.

items.prose: A BFS uses `deque`, but someone wrote `queue.pop()` instead of `queue.popleft()`.
items.question: What happens?

options.text: It still reaches every connected node, but in a depth-first style order, so its rounds no longer mean distances
Nothing changes: both remove one node
options.why: `pop()` removes from the back, the newest node, so the deque acts as a stack.
`deque.pop()` exists and works; it just takes from the other end.

feedback.correct: Back-end removal turns the queue into a stack.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which end each method takes from.

explain.text: `pop()` takes the node added last, so the search dives from the newest node. Every reachable node is still visited once, thanks to `seen`. But the order is no longer level by level.

items.prose:
```python
adj = {"a": ["b", "c"], "b": ["d"], "c": ["d"], "d": ["e"],
       "e": ["f"], "f": ["d", "g"], "g": []}
```
Each list names the tasks that wait for the key.
items.question: How many tasks does Kahn's algorithm emit?

feedback.correct: a, b and c; then d waits on f, which waits on d.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the in-degree counts forward.

byKey.all: d, e and f form a cycle, so none of them reaches in-degree 0, and g waits behind f.
byKey.four: d still has an arrow in from f after b and c are done, so it is never free.

explain.text: d has in-degree 3: from b, c and f. After a, b and c, it still waits on f, and f waits on e, which waits on d. So 3 of 7 tasks are emitted, and g is stuck behind the cycle.

items.prose: A directed graph of trades: an arrow from A to B means A's position feeds B's. Write a reachability check that works on long chains.
items.question: Write `has_path(adj, s, t)`: `True` when following arrows from `s` can reach `t`.

tests.setup: adj = {i: [i + 1] for i in range(5000)}; adj[5000] = []

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on directed graphs, including a node that is its own target, a cycle and a 5,001-node chain. Return `True` or `False`.

feedback.correct: A stack search from `s`, stopping when it pops `t`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 goes against the arrows: C cannot reach A in a directed graph.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 asks whether A reaches itself: a path of length 0 counts.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is a chain of 5,001 nodes. Recursion runs out of frames; use a stack.

explain.text: Any search from `s` visits exactly the nodes it can reach. Checking each popped node against `t` lets it stop early. An explicit stack keeps long chains safe.
